23 Jesus answered and said unto him, If a man love me, he will keep my words: and my Father will love him, and we will come unto him, and make our abode with him. 24 He that loveth me not keepeth not my sayings: and the word which ye hear is not mine, but the Father's which sent me. - John 14:23-24 (KJV)

If you are born again, and truly love Jesus, then you will want to keep His words, and follow all His commandments. If we love Jesus and keep His word, the Father will love us, and the whole God-Head will come and dwell within us. Wow – what a wonderful promise this is, and we become the temple of God, as well as the Holy Spirit and Jesus. This verse does not say that if you want the Father to love you, you must keep the words of Jesus, as that would be works of the law. The whole point is, if you love Jesus and keep His words, then He and the Father will love you. To assure your eternal salvation, you must obey Jesus (Hebrews 5:9), as your name can be blotted out of the book of life (Revelation 3:5).

If you don’t love Jesus, you won’t want to keep His words, so one way to tell if you are born again, and love Jesus, is whether you try to keep His words and commandments. If you say you are born again and yet don’t show any fruit of salvation, then you can’t be telling the truth. If you get born again, your “want to” changes, and you will want to be holy, as He is holy (1 Peter 1:16). The difference between works of the law, and works of faith, is all in the heart attitude, and what your faith is in – whether in your righteousness or in Jesus righteousness. Praise God that He looks on the heart, and He knows what our motivations are, and if we are serving Him out of love or obligation.

Minimum Wage Hike Closes San Francisco Bookstore
This exemplifies the bittersweetness that is raising the minimum wage.

It's sad to see classic businesses go out like a candle in s stormy night, but I doubt this is a problem with with raising minimum wage. Rather, I think it's the increasingly obsolete nature of print. I'm not sure how many vinyl records factories went under the last time they were forced to pay their employees more because of a minimum wage hike... but would you blame it on the hike? or would you blame it on the markets that have an incredibly decreased demand for vinyl records?

In this bookstore's case I am not saying that the raise in minimum wage was the ultimate cause of it closing, but it is at least a proximate one.

One of the main points against raising the minimum wage is that, although it might be good that people get paid more, the raise in minimum wage discourages companies from employing more people. This raises the question: is it better for more people to be employed but have a lower wage, or have less employed, albeit better paid individuals?

That is the age-old question when it comes to any worker's privileges. Balance must be met, I think. Minimum wage is a complicated dance between profits, worker's rights, living wage/cost of living, and many other economy-related things I'm probably ignorant about.

The only three options I see for a business are to ether cut back on staff (or not hire as many people), accept the reduction in profit, or raising the cost of the product/service the business provides. Or a mix of the three. So four, really.

Sure, they could like to hire less people, maybe lay off some people to keep their profits unaffected. But there comes a point that any one worker is over-worked when dealing with all the stuff they're employed to do. When people dont last much time in a position, that is bad for business, because you're periodically spending resources to replace the latest person to burn out quickly in an overloaded work requirement. It may also impact the quality of service, actively costing the business money than they save cutting staff to save the money that would have gone towards the minimum-wage employees.

A reduction in profits would depend on each individual case. It may be a trivial reduction, or one that leads the business to not be profitable or not worth keeping open due to a very small profit margin. Let's say Walmart's profits reduce from (assuming hey dont lay of many workers and continue their hiring practices as usual) $3 million to $2 million on a given place thanks to a minimum wage hike that is still a feasible business model, and they're not shutting down in that state due to an immediate reduction in profit (that may pay off in more sales later on).

Raising cost to adjust for minimum wage is another can of worms I dont feel knowledgeable enough to address. It may offset the good that comes from a raised minimum wage, it may not work for the business and bring it under, it might offset some of the good the minimum wage increase brings but balance out in a way that the minimum wage increase does the good it was intended to do.

It's a large, complicated debate. Raising the minimum wage (I think) is a good idea in most states, but it must be do in a smart way, reasonable, etc.
